title: Psalm 42: As the Deer Pants for Water
summary: Far from the temple, a worshiper thirsts for God like a deer panting for streams. Mocked by people who ask “Where is your God?” and haunted by memories of leading festival crowds to God's house, he speaks to his own downcast soul and tells it to hope in God. The psalm moves between despair and hope, with the same refrain in verses 5 and 11.
story: Psalm 42 opens Book II of the Psalter (Psalms 42 to 72) and begins a group of psalms attributed to the sons of Korah (42 to 49, with Psalm 43 untitled). Book I closed with a doxology after many laments of David; Book II opens with the voice of a Levite singer cut off from the temple where he once led worship. Most scholars think Psalms 42 and 43 were originally a single poem: they share the refrain Why are you downcast, O my soul, Psalm 43 has no heading of its own, and a number of Hebrew manuscripts join them. Read together, they form a three-part lament that ends with the hope of returning to God's altar.
historical:
The heading calls this a Maskil of the sons of Korah. Korah was a Levite who rebelled against Moses and Aaron and died under God's judgment (Numbers 16), but his sons did not die (Numbers 26:11). Their descendants later served in the temple as gatekeepers and singers (1 Chronicles 9:19; 26:1; 2 Chronicles 20:19). The heading probably means the psalm belonged to the repertoire of this Levitical guild, or was composed by one of its members, rather than by the original sons of Korah. Maskil is a term of uncertain meaning, possibly a teaching or skillful psalm.

Verse 6 places the speaker in the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon, far to the north near the sources of the Jordan River, well away from Jerusalem. Mount Mizar is otherwise unknown, and its name means small mountain; some take it as a local peak, others as a play contrasting a little hill with Zion. The setting suggests someone prevented from coming to the temple, whether by illness, exile, or captivity. Suggestions range from a Levite in the northern region during a time of conflict to a deportee taken north by Assyrian or Babylonian armies, but the psalm itself doesn't specify.
cultural:
The deer panting for streams of water pictures an animal in a dry land searching for a stream that may have run dry. In the hills of Israel, seasonal streams (wadis) flowed in the rainy season and dried up in summer. Thirst was a familiar and dangerous experience, and the image suggests desperate need, not mild longing.

Verse 4 recalls pilgrim festivals. Israelite men were to appear before the LORD three times a year, at Passover, Weeks, and Booths (Deuteronomy 16:16), and crowds traveled to Jerusalem singing. The phrase appear in God's presence in verse 2 uses the language of those pilgrimages. As a Levite, the speaker had led these processions. The roar of waterfalls and breakers in verse 7 draws on the torrents that run off Mount Hermon, the tallest peak in the region, whose snowmelt feeds the Jordan. What should be life-giving water here becomes overwhelming, as if the speaker is drowning rather than drinking.
literary: The psalm is built around a refrain in verses 5 and 11 (repeated in Psalm 43:5), in which the speaker addresses his own soul: Why are you downcast. This self-address is unusual and striking. The two stanzas each move from lament to the refrain: verses 1 to 5 center on thirst and memory, and verses 6 to 11 on overwhelming waters and taunts. Water imagery runs throughout, from thirst for streams to floods of tears to breakers crashing over the speaker. The taunt Where is your God appears twice (verses 3 and 10), each time followed by the speaker's struggle to hold on. The psalm uses Elohim (God) far more than the LORD, part of a pattern across Psalms 42 to 83 that scholars call the Elohistic Psalter.

outline.t: Tears, taunts, and memories of festival worship
Refrain: why are you downcast, O my soul
Despair far from Zion, and God's love by day and night
Why have You forgotten me? The enemies' taunt

doctrines.note: The refrain tells the soul to put its hope in God even when feelings say otherwise. Hope here is not a mood but a decision made against the evidence of present circumstances, based on who God is.

The psalm gives words to spiritual depression: tears as food, a downcast soul, a sense of being forgotten by God. It shows that such experiences belong within faith and can be brought to God honestly.
The psalmist prays to God and also speaks to his own soul. Prayer in the Psalms includes preaching to oneself, reminding the heart of what it knows to be true.

words.note: Ayyal, deer or stag. The image of a deer panting for water appears only here in the Psalms, though deer are mentioned elsewhere as symbols of swiftness and grace (Psalm 18:33). The desperate thirst of a wild animal captures the intensity of the psalmist's longing for God.

Tsame, to thirst. In verse 2 the soul thirsts for God, the living God. Thirst is one of the Bible's strongest images for spiritual longing (Psalm 63:1; Isaiah 55:1; John 7:37). Here it is thirst not for blessings but for God himself.

Shachach, to bow down or be brought low. In the refrain it describes the downcast soul. The same verb is used of people bowed in humiliation or grief. The speaker's soul is bent low, and the refrain calls it to look up in hope.

Tehom, the deep, the great waters. It is the same word used in Genesis 1:2 for the deep over which darkness lay. In verse 7 deep calls to deep, as waves and waterfalls overwhelm the speaker. The chaos waters that God mastered at creation seem to be rolling over him, yet he still calls them Your breakers and waves.

christ: Jesus spoke of a thirst for God that he himself satisfies: whoever is thirsty may come to him and drink, and rivers of living water will flow from within (John 7:37-38). The psalm's longing for the living God finds its answer in Christ, who is God present with his people. In Gethsemane Jesus told his disciples that his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Matthew 26:38; Mark 14:34), in words that many interpreters hear as echoing the refrain of Psalms 42 and 43 in the Greek translation. That connection is a verbal echo rather than an explicit quotation, but it suggests that Jesus entered the same anguish of the downcast soul. A taunt much like the one in verses 3 and 10 was flung at him on the cross, when mockers said God should rescue him if God wanted him (Matthew 27:43), and his resurrection became God's answer.
questions: The psalmist compares his longing for God to a deer's thirst for water. When have you felt that kind of thirst?
The refrain has the speaker talking to his own soul. What truths do you need to remind yourself of when you feel downcast?
Memories of past worship bring both comfort and pain in verse 4. How do you handle seasons when worship feels distant?
